name: dB gain
seoDesc: dB gain: work out final power (P₂) from the initial power and the DB gain. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the dB gain calculator the initial power, the DB gain, the initial voltage and the final voltage and it returns final power (P₂). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the dB gain calculator work?
sections.html:
The dB gain calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports final power (P₂) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the initial power (P₁), the DB gain (Power gain in dB), the initial voltage (V₁) and the final voltage (V₂).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in watts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in dB.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the dB gain calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Final power (P₂)=(10, (1 ÷ 10) × DB gain) × initial power (P₁)
DB gain=20 × the natural log of (final voltage (V₂) ÷ initial voltage (V₁)) ÷ the natural log of (10)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial power (P₁) = 10 W and dB gain = 10. The calculator returns Final power (P₂) = 100 W.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Final power (P₂) = 100 W should be roughly the size you expected from Initial power (P₁) = 10 W and dB gain = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in watts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Power, opening in watts
  • Power, opening in watts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Voltage, opening in volts

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The dB gain calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial power, the DB gain and the initial voltage — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the dB gain calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns final power (P₂), derived from the initial power, the DB gain and the initial voltage. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the dB gain calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial power, the DB gain, the initial voltage and the final voltage, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial power (P₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial power (P₁) opens in watts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Final power (P₂) = 100 W. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the dB gain calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
